prize_parts.citation: for discoveries concerning the incretin hormone GLP-1, including the identification and synthesis of its active form, which established the physiological basis for glucose-dependent and weight-reducing therapies

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize on B033 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 showed that the six of us agree on the scientific case, so I want to rest the final position on what has been tested rather than on the count. The chain is complete and independently confirmed: GLP-1 as a glucose-dependent incretin and the proglucagon-derived peptide biology, the identity of the truncated bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide, receptor pharmacology, and then large randomized trials with consistent glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal effects across several agents. This is mature. Durability and long-term safety in obesity are still accumulating, but that is a feature of any successful chronic therapy and is not a reason to withhold recognition of a discovery whose physiological basis is settled. I would word the citation so that it recognises physiology and identification of the active peptide, and does not claim a first discovery of the incretin concept; that concept predates all three laureates and the wording should not imply otherwise.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains the weak point, and I should say plainly that the supplied evidence does not let me resolve Mojsov against Habener and colleagues on first identification of the active peptide. What I can say is that Mojsov's contribution does not depend on being first: the synthesis and characterisation of the active form is a distinct and necessary step, and the citation is worded to rest on that rather than on priority. If the committee judged the record insufficient for Mojsov, I would not substitute Knudsen, because that changes the prize from discovery to development; I would rather consider Drucker and Holst alone, or fall back to B036. A three-name cap also leaves out Knudsen and uncredited early contributors, and I accept that some readers will see that as a cost to translational work. I judge it the lesser unfairness, since recognising the physiology does not diminish the drug development that followed.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius opened with Knudsen in place of Mojsov, withdrew the substitution in round 1 as the weaker choice, and still states lower confidence in the exact trio than in the achievement itself.
responses.response: I appreciate that you moved off Knudsen, and your remaining doubt about the trio is the one I share, so I will not pretend the attribution is resolved. My answer is to separate two questions. Who was first to identify the active peptide is contested and I cannot settle it from the supplied text. Whether Mojsov made a necessary contribution through synthesis and characterisation of the active form is a narrower claim and, as far as the evidence in front of us goes, it holds. On that basis I keep her in the trio and tie the citation to identification and synthesis rather than priority. If you think the narrower claim also fails, I would like to hear which part, because that would move me toward Drucker and Holst only, not toward Knudsen.

responses.point: Sandberg-Rickard considers that a second achievement cannot be added alongside B033 within the three-person cap, and names B036 (Mori and Walter) as the cleaner two-person alternative if attribution on B033 is judged unsettled.
responses.response: I agree that a second part is not feasible: three names are needed for B033, and cutting it to two to make room would worsen the very attribution problem we are worried about. I therefore keep a single part. I also agree that B036 is the right fallback on attribution grounds, but I would be clear about what we trade. It gives us the tidiest credit on the list and a thoroughly confirmed mechanism, while the medical consequences are still prospective. If the B033 attribution were judged intractable I would move to B036, but I do not regard the Mojsov question as intractable, because the citation can be framed to avoid it. So B036 stays an alternative and not my primary choice.

responses.point: Perlmann-Thomas notes that if priority among Holst, Drucker and Mojsov cannot be settled, a configuration that goes to the physiology could look arbitrary, and that Knudsen was decisive in turning the biology into liraglutide and semaglutide.
responses.response: The arbitrariness risk is real, and I do not dismiss it. Where I differ is on how to reduce it. Adding Knudsen would not make the cut less arbitrary; it would replace a discovery rationale with a development rationale and then raise the question of why other medicinal chemists are not included. The more defensible line is a stated principle: the prize recognises the physiological discovery and the identification of the active peptide, and the citation says so. With that principle, Holst and Drucker for the physiology and Mojsov for the active peptide follow without needing to rank anyone's overall importance. I acknowledge, as you do, that this leaves out the people whose drugs patients actually receive, and I would rather say that openly than hide it in the citation.

responses.point: Linnarsson-Sten values B047 (Krainer and Bennett) for its direct line from a splicing mechanism to an approved drug and its two-name credit.
responses.response: I take the force of your argument, and I do not want to belittle antisense correction of SMN2. The two-name attribution is among the cleanest on the list and the clinical effect is dramatic. My hesitation is the one I gave in round 1: the discovery content is narrower and the field is younger, so I think it fits better in a later year. It does not alter my primary position or my two alternatives, but I would not object to it as a future candidate once the platform has matured further.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports Mojsov as first to identify the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, as opposed to Habener and colleagues, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence; my position rests on her synthesis and characterisation of the active form, not on priority.
Whether excluding Knudsen will be read as a judgement against translational work, and whether the citation wording is enough to prevent that reading.
Whether long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 agents in obesity will change the picture; I do not think it justifies deferral, but the data are still accumulating.
Whether B013 can be settled without Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept, which affects its value as my second alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile documents roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy) and a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard. Neither is a candidate here, and no credited name in my configuration or alternatives is documented as a collaborator, so I see no recusal issue. I disclose the Perlmann co-authorship for transparency, and I have responded to his position on its scientific merits.
